blocks.prompt: 1 Models are used to understand problems and make decisions. (i) Define a model and explain it with the map analogy. (2) (ii) Explain how a model helps in decision making, with the farmer's example. (2) (iii) Describe how models are applied in weather forecasting, financial predictions and scientific research. (4) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Model: a model is a simplified way of looking at a complex problem or situation. It helps to understand, explain or predict how things work. Just as a map helps someone navigate a city by showing roads and landmarks, a model helps us understand a problem by focusing on the most important parts and leaving out unnecessary details. Example: a student's study plan is a model that simplifies the schedule by focusing on important subjects.

(ii) Decision making: models give a structured way to think about a problem; they take complicated information and make it easier to work with, and help us consider different outcomes before making a choice. Example: by studying weather patterns and soil conditions, a model helps a farmer predict the right planting time, which increases the chances of a good harvest.

(iii) Applications:
1. Weather forecasting: meteorologists collect data such as temperature, humidity and wind speed, then use models to analyse this data and forecast future weather conditions.
2. Financial predictions: banks and companies use models to predict economic trends, stock prices and even customer behaviour.
3. Scientific research: models help scientists test theories, explore new ideas and make predictions based on data. With advances in Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), models have become even more powerful and accurate in analysing large amounts of data.

book_ref.quote: They are widely used in various fields to make predictions and decisions based on available data

blocks.prompt: 2 Measures of central tendency describe the typical value of data. (i) Define measures of central tendency and name them. (2) (ii) Explain the mean, the median (odd and even number of values) and the mode (one and more modes), finding each for the data 4, 9, 9, 6, 12, 2, 6 and for 4, 9, 9, 6, 12, 2. (6) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Measures of central tendency help us find the centre or typical value in a set of data; they give a sense of the average or most common values. The three main measures are mean, median and mode.

(ii) Mean: the average of all the numbers. Add all the numbers and divide by the total number of values.
Data A (4, 9, 9, 6, 12, 2, 6): sum = 48, mean = 48/7 ≈ 6.86.
Data B (4, 9, 9, 6, 12, 2): sum = 42, mean = 42/6 = 7.

Median: the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order. With an odd number of values it is the exact middle number; with an even number it is the average of the two middle numbers.
Data A in order: 2, 4, 6, 6, 9, 9, 12 (7 values, odd), median = 6 (the 4th value).
Data B in order: 2, 4, 6, 9, 9, 12 (6 values, even), median = (6 + 9)/2 = 7.5.

Mode: the number that appears most often. There can be more than one mode if several numbers share the highest frequency.
Data A: 6 and 9 each appear twice, so there are two modes, 6 and 9.
Data B: only 9 appears twice, so the mode is 9.

book_ref.quote: If there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers

blocks.prompt: 3 Two sections took the same test. Section X scored 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and Section Y scored 40, 55, 65, 80, 90. Define measures of dispersion, then find the variance and standard deviation of both sections and say which section's scores are more spread out. (8 marks)
blocks.explanation: Measures of dispersion tell us how spread out or scattered the data is, i.e. whether the points are close to the mean or far from it. Use σ² = (1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)² and σ = √σ².

book_ref.quote: These help us understand whether the data points are close to the average (mean) or far from it

steps: Section X squared deviations: (−4)² = 16, (−2)² = 4, 0² = 0, 2² = 4, 4² = 16; sum = 40.
Section X variance σ² = 40/5 = 8; standard deviation σ = √8 ≈ 2.83.
Section Y squared deviations: (−26)² = 676, (−11)² = 121, (−1)² = 1, 14² = 196, 24² = 576; sum = 1,570.
Section Y variance σ² = 1,570/5 = 314; standard deviation σ = √314 ≈ 17.72.
Both sections have the same mean (66), but Section Y has a much higher variance, so its scores are more spread out; Section X's scores are closely packed around the mean.
blocks.final_answer: Section X: variance 8, standard deviation ≈ 2.83. Section Y: variance 314, standard deviation ≈ 17.72. Section Y is more spread out.

blocks.prompt: 4 The hours spent on homework in a week by 10 classmates are 3, 5, 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, 15, 16, 18. Calculate the mean, median and mode, and then the variance and standard deviation. State what these values tell about the study habits. (8 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use the central tendency rules, then σ² = (1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)² and σ = √σ².

book_ref.quote: For illustration, you can use the following sample data: 3, 5, 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, 15, 16, 18

steps: Median: the data is already in order; 10 values (even), so median = (10 + 12)/2 = 11 hours.
Mode: 8 and 15 each appear twice, so there are two modes, 8 and 15 hours.
Squared deviations: 64, 36, 9, 9, 1, 1, 16, 16, 25, 49; their sum = 226.
Variance σ² = 226/10 = 22.6.
Standard deviation σ = √22.6 ≈ 4.75 hours.
Reflection: a typical classmate spends about 11 hours; the standard deviation of about 4.75 hours shows that the hours are fairly spread out, from 3 to 18 hours.
blocks.final_answer: Mean = 11 h, median = 11 h, modes = 8 h and 15 h, variance = 22.6, standard deviation ≈ 4.75 h.

blocks.prompt: 5 Statistics summarizes data and predicts outcomes. (i) What are descriptive statistics? Summarize the scores 50, 65, 75, 80, 85, 90, 95, 60, 70, 88 by their mean, highest and lowest score. (4) (ii) Define probability, write its formula, apply it to tossing a coin and name three areas where probability is used. (4) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Descriptive statistics are used to summarize and organize data. Instead of looking at every individual piece of data, they give us a way to see the overall picture.
For the ten scores:
Mean = (50 + 65 + 75 + 80 + 85 + 90 + 95 + 60 + 70 + 88)/10 = 758/10 = 75.8
Highest score = 95; lowest score = 50.
These simple calculations give a quick summary of how the students performed without looking at each score in detail.

(ii) Probability is the study of how likely an event is to happen; it helps us predict outcomes based on what we know.
Probability = number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes
Coin: there are two equally likely outcomes, heads or tails. Probability of heads = 1/2 = 50%, and probability of tails is also 1/2 = 50%.
Uses: predicting the weather, making business decisions and even playing cricket.

book_ref.quote: Probability is the study of how likely an event is to happen

blocks.prompt: 6 Different research needs different ways of gathering data. (i) Define data collection and state what the choice of method depends on. (2) (ii) Explain surveys, observations and experiments, giving the chapter's example of each. (6) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Data collection is the process of gathering relevant information for a particular purpose. The methods are surveys, observations and experiments, each with its own strengths and suitable contexts. Choosing the right method depends on the research objective and the type of data required.

(ii) 1. Surveys: a commonly used method for collecting large amounts of data in a structured way, by asking a predefined set of questions to a sample group. They can be conducted through online forms, telephone calls or face-to-face interviews.
Example: a small grocery store in Islamabad gave a five-question customer preference survey to 50 customers over a weekend and analysed the responses to stock the products customers wanted, improving its business.

2. Observations: data is collected by watching or monitoring subjects in their natural environment. It is useful for gathering data on behaviours or phenomena without interference.
Example: a restaurant staff member watched which tables customers chose at lunchtime for one week; the restaurant then arranged its seating to improve comfort, customer flow and service.

3. Experiments: one or more variables are manipulated to determine their effect on another variable. This is useful in scientific and engineering fields where controlled environments are necessary for accurate measurement.
Example: a teacher gave printed notes to one group of students while the other relied only on lectures; after one month both took the same test and the results were compared.

book_ref.quote: Depending on the nature of the research, different methods can be used for data collection

blocks.prompt: 7 Collected data must be made ready before analysis. (i) What is data preparation? (2) (ii) Explain data cleaning with the school grade records of Table 5.2. (3) (iii) Explain data transformation and differentiate it from data cleaning. (3) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Data preparation: once data has been collected it is prepared for analysis. This includes cleaning the data to remove errors or inconsistencies, organizing it in a meaningful way and converting it into a format suitable for analysis. Where data is missing or incorrect, techniques such as interpolation or statistical adjustments may be used. Proper preparation ensures reliable and valid results.

(ii) Data cleaning means correcting or removing any problems in the data, such as incorrect entries, missing values or duplicate data. If these errors are not fixed, the results of the analysis will be misleading.
Example (Table 5.2): in a school's grade records, the name "Alie" was entered incorrectly and is corrected to "Ali", and Sara's missing grade is found and filled in (75), so the dataset becomes complete.

(iii) Data transformation: once the data is clean, it is transformed into a format that is easy to work with, e.g. by converting data into different formats, creating new columns or organizing data in a different way. This makes the data more suitable for analysis or modelling.

book_ref.quote: It shows examples of common issues such as incorrect names, missing grades, and duplicate entries

rows: Corrects or removes problems in the data.
Changes clean data into a format that is easy to work with.
Deals with incorrect entries, missing values and duplicate data.
Converts formats, creates new columns or organizes data differently.
Done first; unfixed errors give misleading results.
Done after cleaning, to suit analysis or modelling.

blocks.prompt: 8 In a dataset of student grades, Sara's grade is missing. (i) Why is missing data a problem and what does the choice of a technique depend on? (2) (ii) Explain imputation, flagging and removal, applying each to Sara's record, with one advantage or risk of each. (6) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Missing values make the data incomplete; for example, a missing grade makes it hard to assess Sara's performance. Techniques include removing rows with missing values if they are very few, or filling them with an average or with data from similar cases. The choice depends on the type of data and the amount of missing information.

(ii) 1. Imputation: the missing value is estimated using existing data. The school calculates the average grade of Sara's class; if it is 82, this value is assigned to Sara's record temporarily. Advantage: the school keeps a complete dataset while making a reasonable assumption about her performance.

2. Flagging: a note is added in the dataset showing that Sara's grade is not available, so analysts know the data is incomplete. Advantage: it ensures transparency and lets the analysis proceed without filling the gap.

3. Removal: if the number of missing entries is small, Sara's record is excluded from specific analyses. This is acceptable if it does not significantly affect the overall understanding of student performance. Risk: valuable information about Sara is lost.

book_ref.quote: Sometimes, data is incomplete or has missing values

blocks.prompt: 9 Statistical models help in planning a family budget. (i) Define statistical modeling and explain it with the grocery expense example. (3) (ii) Give four suggestions for improving a statistical model and explain why each helps. (5) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Statistical modeling is a way to use data to make sense of the world and predict what will happen in the future. To know how much you will spend on groceries next month, you look at what you spent in the past and, by analysing that data, create a model to estimate future expenses. If you usually spend around 10,000 rupees a month but the amount fluctuates, the model can take into account factors like family size or special occasions, giving a better idea of next month's grocery budget.

(ii) 1. Use more data points: more data gives better accuracy.
2. Include relevant factors, such as family size or special events, that may affect spending, so the model explains the real causes of change.
3. Regularly update the model with new data, to keep it relevant.
4. Test the predictions against actual spending, to find the error and refine the approach.

book_ref.quote: If you usually spend around 10,000 rupees each month, but your expenses fluctuate

blocks.prompt: 10 A tea stall recorded these data for five days (customers, earnings in rupees): (5, 300), (10, 450), (15, 600), (20, 750), (25, 900). Write the simple linear regression formula and explain its terms. Find the slope and intercept, write the final equation, predict the earnings for 22 customers, and find the error if on another day 26 customers gave earnings of 920 rupees. (8 marks)
blocks.explanation: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε, where Y is the dependent variable (earnings), X the independent variable (customers), β₀ the intercept (Y when X = 0), β₁ the slope (change in Y for each unit increase in X) and ε the error term (difference between predicted and actual values).

book_ref.quote: To build a linear regression model, we need data

steps: Slope: for every 5 extra customers the earnings rise by 150 rupees (450 − 300), so β₁ = 150/5 = 30 rupees per customer.
Intercept: take the point (10, 450): 450 = β₀ + 30 × 10 = β₀ + 300, so β₀ = 450 − 300 = 150 rupees.
Final equation: Earnings = 150 + 30 × Customers (150 rupees even with no customers; each customer adds 30 rupees).
Check: 25 customers give 150 + 750 = 900 rupees, which matches the data.
Prediction for 22 customers: 150 + 30 × 22 = 150 + 660 = 810 rupees.
Testing: for 26 customers the model predicts 150 + 30 × 26 = 150 + 780 = 930 rupees.
Error = predicted − actual = 930 − 920 = 10 rupees; the prediction is close but not perfect, because real-world data has some variation.
blocks.final_answer: β₁ = 30, β₀ = 150, Earnings = 150 + 30 × Customers; 22 customers → 810 rupees; error for 26 customers = 930 − 920 = 10 rupees.

blocks.prompt: 11 Logistic regression predicts yes/no outcomes. Explain how logistic regression differs from linear regression and explain the terms of the logistic function. A fitted model is P(pass) = 1 / (1 + e^−(−3 + 1 × Hours Studied)). Find the probability of passing for 2, 3 and 5 hours of study and interpret the results. (8 marks)
blocks.explanation: Logistic regression is used when the outcome is "yes" or "no". Unlike linear regression, it does not predict exact numbers; it gives a probability between 0 and 1. In P(pass) = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + β₁ × Hours Studied)): P(pass) is the probability of passing, e is the base of the natural logarithm, β₀ is the intercept (the log-odds of passing when no hours are studied) and β₁ is the coefficient of hours studied (how much the log-odds change with each additional hour).

book_ref.quote: Instead of giving a specific score, logistic regression helps us find the probability of passing

steps: Here β₀ = −3 and β₁ = 1.
Interpretation: every probability lies between 0 and 1, and since β₁ is positive the chance of passing rises with each extra hour of study.
blocks.final_answer: P(2 h) ≈ 0.27, P(3 h) = 0.5, P(5 h) ≈ 0.88; more study hours give a higher chance of passing.

blocks.prompt: 12 A model is useful only if it performs well and is used responsibly. (i) Differentiate between error metrics and accuracy metrics with an example of each, and explain what interpreting a model's output means. (4) (ii) Explain the ethical considerations of fairness and data privacy in building models. (4) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Performance metrics measure how well a model is doing.
Interpreting a model's output means understanding what the results tell us and drawing conclusions; e.g. if a linear regression model shows that hours studied strongly affect exam scores, we conclude that students should study more hours to improve their scores.

(ii) When building models, ethical implications must be considered:
1. Fairness and bias: a model should be fair and not biased. For example, a model used to decide who gets a loan should not unfairly favour one group of people over another.
2. Data privacy: when personal data is used to build models, privacy must be respected. A company using customer data should ensure the data is secure and not shared without permission.

book_ref.quote: In our grocery example, if the model predicts a monthly grocery bill of 8,000 rupees but the actual bill is 10,000 rupees

rows: Measure how much the predictions differ from the actual values.
Tell how many of the predictions were correct.
Example: predicted grocery bill 8,000 rupees, actual 10,000; the difference (2,000 rupees) is the error.
Example: for a model predicting pass or fail, how often it was right.

blocks.prompt: 13 A retail shop has six customers with monthly spending (groceries, clothing) in $: C1 (150, 100), C2 (200, 150), C3 (100, 50), C4 (80, 20), C5 (160, 90), C6 (40, 10). Using K = 2 with initial centres C2 and C6, carry out K-means clustering with the Euclidean distance until the centres stop changing, and describe the two groups. (8 marks)
blocks.explanation: K-means: choose K, place initial centres, assign each point to the nearest centre (Euclidean distance √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)), recalculate each centre as the average position of its cluster, and repeat until the centres no longer change.

book_ref.quote: Your task is to use K-means clustering to group these customers into two clusters based on their spending habits

steps: Step 1: K = 2. Initial centres: Centre 1 = C2 (200, 150), Centre 2 = C6 (40, 10).
Assignment: C1, C2 and C5 are nearer Centre 1; C3, C4 and C6 are nearer Centre 2.
Every customer stays in the same cluster, so the centres no longer change and the clusters are stable.
Cluster 1 (C1, C2, C5) spends more on both groceries and clothing; Cluster 2 (C3, C4, C6) spends less on both.
blocks.final_answer: Cluster 1 = C1, C2, C5 (centre (170, 113.33), higher spenders); Cluster 2 = C3, C4, C6 (centre (73.33, 26.67), lower spenders).

blocks.prompt: 14 Choosing the right chart makes data easy to understand. (i) Define data visualization and state how it helps. (2) (ii) Choose a suitable visualization for each case and give the reason: comparing sales of different products; temperature over a week; distribution of maths exam scores; hours studied against exam scores; comparing the scores of three classes. (6) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Data visualization is the process of representing data in a visual format, such as graphs or charts. It helps us quickly grasp patterns, trends and insights from data.

(ii) 1. Sales of different products: bar chart. Bar charts are ideal for comparing categories; each bar is a product and its height (or length) shows the sales.
2. Temperature over a week: line graph. Line graphs show trends over time; the points are joined by a line, so the daily rise and fall is easy to see.
3. Distribution of maths exam scores: histogram. It groups the scores into bins or intervals and shows how frequently values occur in each range.
4. Hours studied against exam scores: scatterplot. It displays the relationship between two variables; each point is one student, its position giving both values.
5. Scores of three classes: boxplot (whisker plot). It summarizes each class's distribution by the median, quartiles and potential outliers, showing which class performed better overall.

book_ref.quote: It helps us to quickly grasp patterns, trends, and insights from data

blocks.prompt: 15 A shopkeeper wants to track monthly sales. (i) Why are Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets suitable tools for this? (2) (ii) Write the steps to create a bar chart of monthly sales in Excel or Google Sheets. (4) (iii) How would you interpret a bar chart and a line graph of these sales? (2) (8 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Excel and Google Sheets are tools many people already know; they are widely accessible and provide straightforward methods to create charts and graphs. You can easily enter your data and generate visualizations such as bar charts, line graphs and pie charts with just a few clicks.

(ii) 1. Enter your data: put the months (January, February, ...) in one column and the sales figures for each month in another.
2. Select the data: highlight it by clicking and dragging the mouse over the cells.
3. Choose a chart type: click the Insert tab and select the chart type, here a bar chart.
4. Customize the chart: add labels, e.g. the months on the x-axis and the sales figures on the y-axis, to make the chart clearer and easier to interpret.

(iii) It is important to understand what the chart is telling you. A bar chart compares categories, so it shows which month had the most sales. A line graph shows trends over time, so it shows how sales increased or decreased over several months.

book_ref.quote: Understanding Statistical Representations: When you create a visualization
